profile.reading:
This Meta data center building (building 3 of 3 mapped in this cluster, westernmost to easternmost ordering) is part of Meta's Huntsville campus in Madison County, Alabama. Meta announced the original data center in 2018 with roughly $750 million in investment, calling Huntsville "a natural fit for Facebook," and the facility became operational in 2022, per WHNT's reporting. Meta later announced an expansion that brought total investment in the campus to about $1.5 billion and grew the campus to nearly 3.5 million square feet; the original building was expected to support around 100 jobs, with the expansion adding more than 300 additional positions. Meta's current fact sheet for the campus reports the same $1.5 billion-plus total investment, roughly 300 operational jobs once complete, 1,200 peak skilled-trade construction workers, more than $3.9 million in direct funding to local schools and nonprofits, and a Meta-supported project adding 227 megawatts of new renewable energy in Alabama, alongside Meta's standard 100%-renewable-electricity, LEED Gold, and water-positive-by-2030 commitments. WHNT also reported Meta allocated $600,000 in grants for local STEM programs and teacher-certification initiatives, part of more than $1.5 million contributed to Huntsville-area schools as of 2022. Meta does not publish a specific street address, exact building count, or per-building square footage for individual Huntsville structures beyond the roughly 3.5 million square feet reported campus-wide after expansion; the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates, not from an operator-published source, and should be treated as approximate.

Alabama has permitted data centers to receive combined sales-tax and property-tax abatements for up to 30 years, one of only five states offering that particular combination, and the state hosts more than 20 data center facilities operating or in development, according to reporting on House Bill 399 by the Alabama Reflector. That 2026 legislation, passed by the state Senate, reduces the maximum abatement period to 20 years starting January 1, 2027 (extendable back to 30 years if an operator invests in local infrastructure, broadband, water/wastewater systems, or education), requires data centers drawing 100 megawatts or more to begin paying state sales and use taxes, and extends the overall incentive program's sunset date from 2028 to 2032; the current eligibility threshold for combined incentives is a $400 million investment creating at least 20 jobs paying $40,000 or more annually, a bar Meta's Huntsville investment clears many times over. Alabama does not publicly disclose which specific companies receive these abatements or how much tax revenue is foregone, so this session did not confirm Meta's specific incentive terms for the Huntsville campus beyond the statewide policy framework described in this reporting.

profile.campus: Stanton Springs, Newton County, Georgia (Meta's Stanton Springs data center campus, roughly 40 miles east of Atlanta)
profile.address: Shire Parkway, Newton County, Georgia, 30025
profile.reading:
This building is Meta's Stanton Springs data center (formerly called the Newton Data Center), located in the Stanton Springs development in Newton County, Georgia, about 40 miles east of downtown Atlanta near Social Circle. Facebook announced the project with $750 million in investment for a two-building, 970,000-square-foot campus, and Data Center Frontier reported the facility was fully operational by 2020; at the time of Meta's own March 2021 announcement recapping the project, it was described as Meta's 12th data center globally and 9th in the United States. Meta secured 100% renewable power for the site through a partnership with Walton Electric Membership Corporation, which committed to installing hundreds of megawatts of new solar generation on the Georgia grid to match the facility's electricity use, part of what a Meta representative described as a "renewable energy solution" and "strong partners" being key to the site-selection process. Meta's own materials describe an economic multiplier of roughly 5 jobs supported elsewhere in the local economy per data center job, and about 14.5 jobs per $1 million of capital expenditure, alongside hundreds of construction and trades jobs during the building phase and ongoing engineering and facility-management roles. The site joined a broader hyperscale cluster in the region alongside Switch and CyrusOne, both of which have also expanded data center operations in the same part of Georgia. Meta does not publish a specific street address, exact building count, or per-building square footage; the 970,000-square-foot figure is a campus-wide total across two buildings, not confirmed per building, and the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates rather than an operator-published source.

Meta's current fact sheet-level materials for its Georgia operations describe the same standard LEED Gold, net-zero, and water-positive-by-2030 commitments applied across its US campuses, alongside the Walton EMC renewable partnership described above as central to why Meta selected the Stanton Springs site.

profile.campus: Altoona, Polk County, Iowa (Meta's Altoona data center campus, seven Meta-tagged buildings on OpenStreetMap; Meta's own reporting describes the campus as still expanding)
profile.address: Share Way, Altoona Meta Data Center, Altoona, Polk County, Iowa, 50009
profile.reading:
This is Facebook/Meta Altoona Data Center 1, the first building on Meta's Altoona, Iowa campus, tied to Meta's original 2013 groundbreaking on the site. Meta has since expanded the campus seven times, most recently announced in December 2024, per Meta's own fact sheet and Data Center Frontier's reporting; Meta has invested more than $2.5 billion in the city of Altoona and the state of Iowa through this campus. Construction has employed an average of about 1,000 workers a year over twelve years, totaling 8.7 million work-hours, with peak skilled-trade staffing of 1,300 workers; day-to-day operations employ more than 400 people. Meta reports operational buildings on the campus are LEED Gold certified, that it matches all of its global electricity use with 100% clean and renewable energy, and that a Meta-supported project added 225 megawatts of new renewable generation capacity in Iowa. Meta says it has made more than 300 grants and sponsorships in the area since 2015 and provided more than $5.6 million in direct funding to Polk County-area schools and nonprofits. Meta does not publish a specific street address, building count, or per-building square footage for individual Altoona structures; the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates, not from an operator-published source, and should be treated as approximate.

Iowa has drawn more than $17 billion in data center capital investment, with 27 data centers operating or under construction statewide as of 2025, according to Inside Climate News; Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Apple together account for nearly all of that total. The state has led the nation in wind generation since adopting the first state renewable portfolio standard in 1983, with wind now supplying about 60% of Iowa's electricity and helping keep industrial power prices among the eighth-lowest in the country, both factors regional reporting ties directly to hyperscale operators' site selection in the Altoona/Des Moines corridor. That same reporting states Meta's Altoona campus has used up to 16% of the city of Altoona's water supply and consumed roughly 1.2 million megawatt-hours of electricity annually, and flags that federal cuts to clean-energy tax incentives under the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act are projected by Energy Innovation to raise Iowa industrial electricity rates by 14 to 26 percent, a risk regional press has connected to the pace of further hyperscale investment in the state.

Meta does not publish a specific street address, current building count, or per-building square footage for individual Gallatin structures beyond the original 982,000-square-foot building reported at announcement; the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates, not from an operator-published source, and should be treated as approximate.

This Meta data center building (building 3 of 3 mapped in this cluster) is part of Meta's Henrico campus at the White Oak Technology Park near Richmond, Virginia. To supply renewable power, Dominion Energy Virginia created a new tariff, Schedule RF, specifically to let large customers like Facebook fund dedicated Virginia solar generation without shifting costs to other ratepayers; Facebook said it funded 500 megawatts of new Virginia solar capacity to source the Henrico center's power as 100% renewable energy, with strong political backing at the time from Governor Terry McAuliffe's administration. Meta's own current fact sheet for the campus reports LEED Gold certification and Meta's standard net-zero, 100%-renewable, and water-positive-by-2030 commitments. Meta does not publish a specific street address, exact current building count, or per-building square footage beyond the original 970,000-square-foot Phase 1 figure; the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates, not from an operator-published source, and should be treated as approximate.

Meta has continued expanding at White Oak: in October 2022 it purchased 475 acres at 3951 Portugee Road for $35.3 million under the internal code name "Project Tropical" (following the earlier "Project Echo" naming), more than doubling its White Oak holdings to just over 800 acres, after roughly 326 acres acquired between 2017 and 2020 for about $13.4 million, according to Richmond BizSense's reporting on county planning filings. Conceptual plans filed with Henrico County called for two additional data centers and three auxiliary buildings on the wooded parcel directly south of Meta's existing facility, by then described in county filings as roughly 2.4 million square feet. Henrico's attractiveness for the expansion was tied by that reporting to the area's proximity to transatlantic subsea internet cables landing at Virginia Beach and to the county's decision to cut its data-center tax rate by about 88 percent, to 40 cents per $100 of assessed value.
